fullText:
有人用AI把物理教材变成了3D交互式教材，学生可以通过预测、动手操作、验证来理解物理规律

目前覆盖动能、重力势能、弹性势能、热传递、功率、效率、能量守恒等，对齐的是英国GCSE物理教材

比如说学动能，学生可以先预测质量或速度增加后动能如何变化，再通过交互式模拟实验检验自己的判断

这种形式比单纯记公式、做题、靠想象更容易建立直觉

有的时候学生记住了公式，也会做题，但不一定真正理解了公式描述的物理规律

这个3D交互教材的最大价值是“预测—测试—验证”体系，学生先提出自己的判断，再通过操作实验验证，让学生自己参与知识发现的过程，抽象概念可视化，把教育从答案引擎式带向了学习体验引擎式

之前发的那个AI教育项目，把教材知识做成图谱，解决“应该学什么、先学什么”的问题，这个3D交互教材解决“怎样才能理解”的问题

如果把两者串接起来，教育或许能从围绕教材、章节、题目的标准教学，变成按理解程度提供个性化学习

项目来自 @techartist_

AMAZON SUMMARY:

The field of artificial intelligence, data science, and analytics is crippling itself. Exaggerated promises of unrealistic technologies, simplifications of complex projects, and marketing hype are leading to an erosion of trust in one of our most critical approaches to making decisions: data driven.

This book aims to fix this by countering the AI hype with a dose of realism. Written by two experts in the field, the authors firmly believe in the power of mathematics, computing, and analytics, but if false expectations are set and practitioners and leaders don’t fully understand everything that really goes into data science projects, then a stunning 80% (or more) of analytics projects will continue to fail, costing enterprises and society hundreds of billions of dollars, and leading to non-experts abandoning one of the most important data-driven decision-making capabilities altogether.

For the first time, business leaders, practitioners, students, and interested laypeople will learn what really makes a data science project successful. By illustrating with many personal stories, the authors reveal the harsh realities of implementing AI and analytics.

fullText:
"Vector: A Surprising Story of Space, Time, and Mathematical Transformation"

Find it here: https://t.co/6vomnSEvTS

Amazon description:

A celebration of the seemingly simple idea that allowed us to imagine the world in new dimensions—sparking both controversy and discovery. 

Vector and tensor calculus offers an elegant language for expressing the way things behave in space and time, and Robyn Arianrhod shows how this enabled physicists and mathematicians to think in a brand-new way. These include James Clerk Maxwell when he ushered in the wireless electromagnetic age; Einstein when he predicted the curving of space-time and the existence of gravitational waves; Paul Dirac, when he created quantum field theory; and Emmy Noether, when she connected mathematical symmetry and the conservation of energy. 

It turned out that it’s not just physical quantities and dimensions that vectors and tensors can represent, but other dimensions and other kinds of information, too. This is why physicists and mathematicians can speak of four-dimensional space-time and other higher-dimensional “spaces,” and why you’re likely relying on vectors or tensors whenever you use digital applications such as search engines, GPS, or your mobile phone.

Anthropic 招股书最快今天公开：拟 11 月中旬上市，募资最高约 1000 亿美元

据 The Information 报道，Anthropic 最早在美国时间 10 月 26 日周一公开 IPO 招股书（S-1）。招股书是公司上市前必须交给美国证监会的一份完整账本，收入、亏损、大客户、合作方分成、谁掌握控制权都要写进去。Anthropic 6 月 1 日已经保密递交过草稿，只有监管能看；公开之后，普通投资者才第一次能完整翻它的账。

截至北京时间 26 日上午，美国证监会的 EDGAR 文件系统里还查不到这份招股书。上周也有报道说它最快 23 日周五公开，最后没有兑现。

【时间表】

据金融媒体 IFR 10 月 15 日报道，Anthropic 计划 26 日公开递交，11 月 9 日开始路演（向机构投资者推介股票），随后一周定价，11 月中旬挂牌。募资目标最高约 1000 亿美元，对应估值约 2 万亿美元，摩根士丹利和高盛牵头承销。这些都来自知情人士，Anthropic 没有公开确认。

这一周也是财报周：微软、Alphabet（谷歌母公司）周三发财报，亚马逊周四发。这三家都和 Anthropic 签了云算力合同，亚马逊和谷歌还是它的大投资方。

【已经流出的数字】

下面这些数字分别来自媒体看到的保密草稿和一场投资者会，都还没经过公开招股书确认，口径可能调整。

收入：据《华尔街日报》看到的一份较新草稿，2026 年上半年收入 163 亿美元，去年同期是 11 亿。第三季度的数字不在草稿里，据 FT 和路透报道，是 Anthropic 10 月 14 日在旧金山总部向潜在投资者介绍的：三季度收入约 168 亿美元，比二季度的 116 亿增长约 45%。这个 45% 是跟上一季度比，一个季度的收入已经超过整个上半年。增速在放缓，二季度比一季度（约 47 亿）涨了约 147%。

亏损：同一份草稿显示，上半年按会计准则净亏损 807 亿美元，其中约 720 亿来自可转债等融资工具的账面调整，没有对应的现金流出。Anthropic 对投资者说，按它自己的口径已连续两个季度盈利，但没说剔除了哪些成本。

对云巨头的依赖：据路透 9 月底看到的保密草稿，2025 年约 47% 的销售（约 21.6 亿美元）是通过亚马逊和谷歌的云市场卖出的。云市场相当于云厂商开的应用商店，企业在 AWS 或谷歌云的账单里直接买 Claude，平台从中抽成。路透估算两家抽走约 3.51 亿美元，相当于每卖 1 美元抽 16 美分。草稿还显示，有两个没有点名的客户各占 2025 年收入的 12%。

这几家云伙伴同时也是 Anthropic 的算力供应商。据《华尔街日报》，草稿列出的未来十年云算力承诺约 4500 亿美元，其中谷歌云 1110 亿、AWS 1100 亿、微软 310 亿。

I actually haven’t understood why people find Convey’s Game of Life so interesting. There are inumberable other constructs in mathematics that give rise to arbitrary complexity from even more simplicy. 

For example, there are extremely simple formulas for pi which in effect are generating perfectly random digits (aka infinite complexity) where there exists all finite programs, all finite subsequence. 

In all cases, it turns out arbitrary complexity doesn’t just rise from simplicity. The apparent simplicity is at best deceptive. For example,  the complexity in digits of pi can be traced down to the fact that linear sequence of integers *also* includes sequence of prime numbers. In most such constructions, the source of virtually all of the complexity can be attributed to prime numbers.

fullText:
Tony Xu of @DoorDash on getting rejected by investors, competing against rivals with thousands of times more capital, and how founders can tell conviction from delusion:

"I had over 100 rejections in a span of over 1,000 days where the company almost constantly ran out of money... I couldn't raise a dime, and we were running out of capital."

"Companies like Amazon or Uber were in the space who had way more capital than we had. Hundreds of times, maybe thousands of times of capital deployed versus the amount that we raised. So then the question becomes, well, how are you gonna win this cash-burning machine?"

"This is where you as the founder have to finely tune that line between delusion and knowing that you have something that others don't understand. What are the customers telling you?"

"We the founders did deliveries for almost virtually every day the first three years of the company's life... And so we had strong points of view on each side of our marketplace that could explain what was happening in the numbers."

"When you have one set of facts, which is your customers, you have another set of facts, what are called opinions and perceptions, you gotta trust the facts. That's ultimately what kept us going."

fullText:
Shigeru Miyamoto (Nintendo) received Japan's prestigious Order of Culture and used the press conference to talk about generative AI, what 'creating' actually means when tools automate execution, and why Kyoto (not Silicon Valley) produced Nintendo's design philosophy.

https://t.co/OtveOcQUX0

The Order of Culture (文化勲章) is one of Japan's highest honors, previously given to film directors like Akira Kurosawa and writers like Yasunari Kawabata. Japan basically put games in the same category as film and literature.

He talks about generative AI in a way I have not seen from many working creators. He distinguishes between "creating" and "working." Creation is the hard part: composition, direction, deciding what should exist. Work is execution, and work is satisfying in a way that can fool you into thinking you have created something.

He says even before AI, tools have always automated technique, from typewriters to desktop publishing. What gets exposed when that happens is whether you had vision and intent, or whether you were just good at execution. AI is doing the same thing at a larger scale, and he finds this encouraging.

"The scary thing is becoming satisfied with the work and mistakenly thinking you created something."

People told him for decades that he should go outside of Japan and be in a "global hub". He stayed in Kyoto anyway. His work became more successful overseas than at home. The reason, he says, is that the person on the other side of the screen is human, regardless of geography. Deep local rootedness kept him anchored in concrete experience rather than trend-following.
